title: The Emperor of Athletes: Louis Apollon (Legends of the Past)
summary: Episode 3 of Legends of the Past profiles French strongman Louis Uni (Louis Apollon, born 1862): his family of giants, childhood labour strength, the Apollon wheels, grip feats and the escaping-prisoner act. NH uses him as proof of how far natural human potential goes, while noting his laziness, lack of showmanship, exploitation by others and early death from smoking.
claims: Old-time strongmen and bodybuilders overlapped far more than today, and natural strongmen of that era are valid inspiration for modern naturals
Louis Uni (nicknamed Apollon) was born in France in 1862 into a family of giants; his grandfather was 6'8 at a time when the average French man was about 5'4
As an 11-12 year old field labourer Apollon carried bags of sea salt weighing a couple hundred pounds, and he pressed loaded cartwheels overhead for reps
At 16 Apollon was 6'3 and about 250 lb before steroids existed; modern YouTube fitness would call those stats unnatural
Apollon shows that the limits of natural human potential are far beyond what people assume
He was fast and athletic, not just a brute: as an amateur he wrestled professionals and never lost a match
Apollon could pinch grip a custom 175-180 lb block of iron, a documented feat few modern strongmen could match even on drugs
He snatched a 180 lb weight one-handed to arm's length and held it there for time; audience members could not even lift it off the ground
In his shows audience members and rival strongmen could challenge him for money, and nobody ever beat him; rivals eventually came just to watch
Apollon built his own weights from junkyard scrap; his famous Apollon wheels were two railway wheels on a thick axle weighing 366 lb, carried home by hand and now kept in a French museum
Because of his gigantic hands Apollon was for a long time the only person who could even grip the thick-handled Apollon wheels
Despite carrying a lot of fat he had a lower-back six-pack showing through, a massive upper back and huge biceps
Unlike torso-dominant modern strongmen, Apollon was limb dominant with calves over 20 inches and 18-inch forearms
He recommends Edmond Desbonnet's book on old strongmen (Les Rois de la Force), which shows natural strength and physique excellence already existed back then
In the escaping-prisoner act Apollon bent iron bars to squeeze through; when a blacksmith secretly hardened the bars he only succeeded after his wife screamed at him, then had to stop the show
Apollon was lazy: he mostly lifted around 80% of his max to avoid struggling and never trained outside his childhood labour and the shows themselves
Apollon made lifts look so easy that audiences thought they were tricks; laypeople cannot tell a 300 lb deadlift from a 700 lb one
Being strong was not enough in that era: lacking showmanship and money drive, Apollon never got the fame his strength deserved
A great physique without an assertive personality invites exploitation; people took advantage of Apollon's kindness and naivety
His career ended when he was badly injured holding back two cars pulling ropes looped around his arms, at a time without effective surgery
Apollon died young of throat cancer as a lifelong smoker: great genetics do not excuse neglecting your health
Whatever genetic cards you are dealt you still have to play the game intelligently; if the lazy Apollon achieved so much, imagine applying yourself
